parts.title: Part 1. Complete the text. Each missing word appears somewhere else in the text.
parts.text: Every Sunday morning, a small market appears in the square in front of the old mosque. Farmers from nearby villages arrive early with their vegetables, fruit and fresh bread. By eight o'clock the square is full of people, and the smell of bread fills the air. Many families come to the {{1}} not only to shop but also to meet friends. Prices are usually lower than in the supermarket, and the {{2}} are often happy to give a better price if you buy a lot. One of the most popular stalls belongs to an old farmer who sells honey from his own bees. He lets visitors taste the {{3}} before they buy it. Children love the stall next to his, where a young woman sells hot {{4}} with cheese. In autumn there is even more {{5}}: melons, grapes and apples cover every table. For many people in the town, a Sunday without a short walk to the market is not a real Sunday, and they {{6}} their friends there every week.

parts.title: Part 2. Read the article and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
At nineteen, Jasur Rakhimov has already built an app used by more than fifty thousand people. The idea came from a problem in his own family. His grandmother, who lives alone in a village near Samarkand, often forgot to take her medicine, and Jasur's mother worried about her constantly. 'There were reminder apps already,' Jasur explains, 'but they were all in English or Russian, and the buttons were too small for older people.'

Jasur taught himself programming from free online videos while he was still at school. His first version of the app was, in his words, 'terrible'. It crashed often, and the reminders sometimes came at the wrong time. Instead of giving up, he asked his grandmother and her neighbours to test each new version and tell him exactly what confused them. 'They were the best teachers I ever had,' he says. 'They didn't care about clever features. They wanted large letters, a loud sound and instructions in Uzbek.'

The app is free to download. Jasur earns a small income from a version for pharmacies, which can send messages to customers when their medicine is ready. He admits that the business is not making him rich, and that he has turned down an offer from a larger company to buy it. 'If I sell it, they might add advertising or make people pay,' he says. 'My grandmother's friends would stop using it.'

Next year Jasur plans to study computer science abroad, but he intends to keep improving the app. 'My grandmother still sends me her ideas,' he laughs. 'Some of them are actually very good.'

parts.title: Part 3. Choose the best heading for each paragraph. There are two headings you do not need.

headings.text: Ask for a higher salary straight away

paragraphs.text: Interviewers are rarely impressed by candidates who know nothing about them. Spend an hour on the company's website and recent news. Find out what it sells, who its customers are and what problems it might be facing. You can then link your experience to the company's real needs rather than speaking in general terms.

Knowing what you want to say is not the same as being able to say it clearly under pressure. Ask a friend to play the interviewer and answer common questions aloud, such as why you want the job. You will quickly notice which answers are too long and which words you keep repeating.

There is no single correct outfit. A bank may expect a suit, while a design studio might find one strange. Look at photos of staff on the company's social media and choose clothes that are slightly smarter than what they wear every day. Whatever you choose, make sure it is clean and comfortable.

Arriving late and out of breath is a terrible way to begin. Check the address the day before, find out how long the trip takes at that time of day and leave extra time for traffic. If possible, aim to be near the building fifteen minutes early, and use the time to calm down.

Most interviews end with the words 'Do you have any questions for us?' Saying no can suggest a lack of interest. Have two or three questions ready, for example about training or what a typical week looks like. Avoid anything you could easily have found out by reading the website.

Within a day of the interview, send a short, polite email to the people you met. Mention one thing from the conversation that made you more interested in the job. It takes five minutes, but many candidates forget, so it can help you stand out.

parts.title: Part 4. Read the text and choose the correct answer.
parts.text:
Few people today are ever truly bored. A spare minute in a queue or on a bus is filled almost automatically by a phone, and the feeling of having nothing to do has become something to be eliminated as quickly as possible. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that in getting rid of boredom we may be losing something valuable.

Their argument rests on what boredom actually does. Far from being a passive state, boredom is an uncomfortable signal that our current activity is not meeting our needs. Like hunger, it pushes us to search for something better. In a well-known experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, later produced more creative ideas than a group who had gone straight to the creative task. The researchers suggested that boredom had encouraged the participants' minds to wander, and that mind-wandering allowed unexpected connections to form.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that more boredom is always better. Chronic boredom, the kind experienced by people trapped in meaningless jobs or with no control over their days, is associated with poorer mental health rather than with creativity. The benefit seems to depend on the boredom being temporary and on the person having the freedom to act on the restlessness it produces.

This is where smartphones change the picture. The problem is not that phones are entertaining, but that they offer relief so quickly that the restlessness never has time to do its work. The mind is pulled back into a stream of content before it has wandered anywhere interesting. Some writers recommend 'boredom breaks': short periods, perhaps on a walk or a bus journey, when the phone stays in the bag and the mind is left to its own devices.

Whether such advice will be widely followed is doubtful. Most people find boredom unpleasant, and technology companies are very good at offering alternatives. But for anyone who struggles to find new ideas, the occasional empty moment may be worth more than it seems.

options.text: A boring task can lead to more creative thinking.

options.text: When it lasts only a short time.
When it is long-term and people have little control.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main concern about smartphones?

options.text: They end restlessness before it can be useful.
They are too expensive for students.

questions.prompt: How does the writer see the chances of 'boredom breaks' becoming popular?

options.text: Unlikely, although the idea has value.

parts.title: Part 2. Listen to a museum guide. Complete the notes with ONE word or a number.
parts.script: Good morning and welcome to the Museum of Applied Arts. My name is Nilufar and I'll be your guide today. Before we start, a few practical points. The tour lasts about ninety minutes and we'll visit three halls. The building itself was built in the nineteenth century as the home of a wealthy diplomat, so please look up at the ceilings: they're decorated with traditional painted patterns. In the first hall you'll see embroidery called suzani, mostly from Bukhara and Nurata. The second hall is dedicated to ceramics, and the third to jewellery and wood carving. You are welcome to take photographs, but please don't use the flash, because strong light can damage the old fabrics. Halfway through the tour we'll stop for ten minutes in the courtyard, where there's a small cafe. At the end, the museum shop sells copies of some items, and all the money goes to restoration work. If you get lost, the exit is always signed in green. Right, please follow me.

parts.title: Part 3. Listen to a radio interview. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
Presenter: My guest today is Malika Yusupova, who started a free running group in Tashkent three years ago. Malika, how did it begin?
Malika: Quite by accident. I used to run alone in the park every Saturday, and a neighbour asked if she could join me. The next week she brought two friends, and it grew from there. Now we have around two hundred people on a good day.
Presenter: That's a lot of people. Do you need to be fit to join?
Malika: Not at all. That's the main thing I want people to understand. We have groups for every speed, including walkers. Some of our members couldn't run for one minute when they started.
Presenter: What keeps people coming back?
Malika: Honestly, it's less about the running than the company. People make friends, they have breakfast together afterwards. For some older members, it's the only time in the week they meet new people.
Presenter: Has it been difficult to organise?
Malika: The hardest part was safety. When we got bigger, we had to agree with the park managers on a route that doesn't cross any roads, and we trained volunteers in first aid.
Presenter: And what's next for the group?
Malika: We'd like to start a similar group in Samarkand. A few people there have already contacted us. But we don't want to grow too fast; the friendly atmosphere is what makes it work.

parts.title: Part 4. Listen to a short talk. Choose the correct answer.
parts.script:
In this short talk I'd like to consider why languages borrow words from one another, and why people often feel so strongly about it. Every language does it. English took thousands of words from French after the eleventh century, and Uzbek contains layers of Persian, Arabic and Russian vocabulary. More recently, almost every language has absorbed English words connected with technology.
The most obvious reason for borrowing is necessity. When a new object or idea arrives, it often brings its name with it, and it is simply easier to adopt that name than to invent a new one. But necessity alone doesn't explain everything. Many borrowed words replace perfectly good existing ones. Here the motive is usually prestige: speakers associate the source language with something desirable, such as modernity, education or wealth, and using its words lends them a little of that status.
This is precisely what tends to upset language purists. Their objection is rarely that the new words are hard to understand; it's that borrowing seems to signal a loss of confidence in one's own culture. Some governments have tried to respond by creating official native alternatives. The results are mixed. A replacement succeeds when it is short, easy to say and introduced early, before the borrowed word becomes established. Once a borrowing is in everyday use, official alternatives usually end up in dictionaries but not in people's mouths.
It's worth remembering, though, that borrowed words don't stay foreign for long. They are adapted to the sounds and grammar of the new language, often change their meaning, and within a generation or two most speakers no longer think of them as borrowed at all. From a historical point of view, borrowing is less a sign of a language's weakness than of its contact with the world.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the first part of the talk?

options.text: To show that all languages borrow words.

questions.prompt: What usually explains borrowing that replaces existing words?
What do purists mainly object to?

options.text: Borrowed words are hard to understand.
What borrowing seems to say about cultural confidence.

questions.prompt: When are official alternatives most likely to succeed?

options.text: When they are introduced before the borrowed word spreads.
When they are longer and more formal.

questions.prompt: What happens to borrowed words over time?

options.text: They become a normal part of the language.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's overall view?

options.text: Borrowing should be controlled by law.
Borrowing reflects contact with other cultures.

input.from: Gulnora Saidova, Events Coordinator, City Youth Centre
input.subject: Language exchange evenings: new arrangements
input.body:
Dear volunteers,

Because of building repairs, our Thursday language exchange evenings will move to the second floor of the central library for the next three months. The sessions will be shorter, ninety minutes instead of two hours, and we can only accept thirty participants each time. Please let us know how you feel about these changes and whether you have any suggestions to help us organise the evenings.

Gulnora Saidova
